Thus it suffices for us to bound $\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}d\mu(x)$ . We follow the idea in the proof of Proposition 9 in [19], and use the observation that for any $C>0$ and $f,f_{-}\in\mathcal{L}_{2}(\mu)$ where $f_{-}\leqslant f$ pointwise, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mu(f)-C\mu_{X^{n}}(f) \displaystyle=\resizebox{21479355}{}{$(\mu(f)-\mu(f_{-}))+(\mu(f_{-})-C\mu_{X^{n}}(f_{-}))+C(\mu_{X^{n}}(f_{-})-\mu_{X^{n}}(f))$} \displaystyle\leqslant(\mu(f)-\mu(f_{-}))+(\mu(f_{-})-C\mu_{X^{n}}(f_{-})), $$

where we used the fact that $f_{-}\leqslant f$ pointwise to derive the inequality above. Now, consider setting

$$ \displaystyle f(x)=\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}, \displaystyle f_{-}(x)=\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}-\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}, $$

where $\Pi_{r}$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{r}\}\subset\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}$ which are the first $r$ eigenfunctions in the Mercer expansion of $k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)$ (so each $e_{i}$ satisfies $\|e_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}=1$ ), and $\Pi_{r,\perp}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the complement of $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{r}\}$ in $\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}$ . We first note that $f_{-}(x)\leqslant f(x)$ holds pointwise by the triangle inequality. Continuing from (56), picking $C=2$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\ \mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})-2\mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}) \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}) \displaystyle\ -\mu\left(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}-\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\right) \displaystyle\ +\mu\left(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}-\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\right) \displaystyle\ -\resizebox{20348790}{}{$2\mu_{X^{n}}\left(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}-\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\right)$} \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ 2\mu\left(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\right) \displaystyle\ +\!\!\mu\!\left(\!\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\!\!\right)\!\!-\!2\mu_{X^{n}}\!\left(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\!\!\right)\! \displaystyle\ +2\mu_{X^{n}}\left(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\right) $$

From (57), we see that we need to bound three terms. The first term we need to bound is $2\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})$ . By nonexpansiveness of $P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 2\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})\leqslant 2\mu(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}) \displaystyle\leqslant 2\sqrt{\mu(\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}^{2})}=2\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}e_{j}(x)^{2}}=2\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}. $$

Next we bound

$$ \left(\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})-2\mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})\right). $$

To do so, we apply Lemma 15 (by picking $C=2$ in that proposition) , which shows that there exists $c>0$ such that for any $\delta>0$ , with probability at least $1-\delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left(\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})-2\mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})\right) \displaystyle\leqslant c\left(\frac{r^{2}\max\{\log(n/r^{2}),1\}}{n}+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}\right). $$

Finally, to bound $\mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})$ , we use Bernstein’s inequality [49]. It suffices to bound $\mu_{X^{n}}(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}$ since $\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}\leqslant\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}$ . Next, observe that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})\leqslant\mu\left(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}^{2}\right)=\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}. $$

Then, since $0\leqslant\sqrt{(k_{\alpha}-\hat{k}_{\alpha,m}^{n})(x,x)}\leqslant\sqrt{k_{\alpha}(x,x)}\leqslant 1$ for any $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , by Bernstein’s inequality, there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\delta>0$ , with probability at least $1-\delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{X^{n}}(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})-\mu(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}) \displaystyle\leqslant c\log(1/\delta)\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})}/\sqrt{n}+1/n\right) \displaystyle\leqslant c\log(1/\delta)\left(\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}/\sqrt{n}+1/n\right) $$

Since $\mu(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})\leqslant\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}$ (this follows from (58)), we thus have (with probability at least $1-\delta)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\ \mu_{X^{n}}(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}) \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \mu(\|\Pi_{r,\perp}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})+c\log(1/\delta)\left(\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}/\sqrt{n}+1/n\right) \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}+c\log(1/\delta)\left(\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}/\sqrt{n}+1/n\right). $$

Thus, by plugging (58), (59) and (60) into (57), we find that

$$ \displaystyle\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}})-2\mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}) \displaystyle\leqslant c\log(1/\delta)\left(\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}+\frac{r^{2}\max\{\log(n/r^{2}),1\}}{n}\right). $$

By picking $r\geqslant\lfloor(2\log n)^{h}/\beta^{h}\rfloor$ and the argument in Remark 1 in [19], using the decay assumption on $\{\sigma_{j}\}$ , we have that

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{j>r}\sigma_{j}}+\frac{r^{2}\max\{\log(n/r^{2}),1\}}{n}=O\left(\frac{(\log n)^{2h+1}}{n}\right) $$

Thus, to bound $\mu(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}),$ all it remains is to bound $2\mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\alpha}}}$ . To this end, observe that

$$ \displaystyle\ \mu_{X^{n}}(\|P_{m,\perp}^{X^{n}}k_{\alpha}(x,\cdot)\|)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{(k_{\alpha}-\hat{k}_{\alpha,m}^{n})(x_{i},x_{i})} \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{(k_{\alpha}-\hat{k}_{\alpha,m}^{n})(x_{i},x_{i})}^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i>m}\lambda_{i}}, $$

where the first inequality follows from Jensen’s, and the second follows from Lemma 2 in [19]. The result then follows by plugging in (62) and (63) into (61), and using the assumption that $m\geqslant\lfloor(2\log n)^{h}/\beta^{h}\rfloor$ as well as the argument in Remark 1 in [19], which by the decay assumption on the empirical eigenvalues gives us $\sqrt{\sum_{i>m}n^{-1}\lambda_{i}}=O\left(n^{-1}(\log n)^{h/2}\right).$ ∎

#### Remark 4.

Our result significantly strengthens the high-probability result in Corollary 1 of [19], since we attain an $O(1/n)$ high-probability rate rather than their $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ rate.

#### Remark 5.

We note that by Theorem 2 in [43], both the (normalized) empirical and Mercer eigenvalues ( $\frac{1}{n}\lambda_{j}$ and $\sigma_{j}$ respectively) satisfy $\lambda_{i}/n\leqslant C^{\prime}\exp(-Ci^{1/d})$ and $\sigma_{i}\leqslant C^{\prime}\exp(-Ci^{1/d})$ for some measure-independent constants $C,C^{\prime}>0$ , where $d$ is the dimension of $\mathcal{S}$ . This justifies our assumption on eigenvalue decay in the statement of Lemma 11. To model cases where the decay exponent may be better than $d$ , we use a general spectral decay exponent $h$ .

### VI-D Detailed Proof for Proposition 3

For notational ease, we define $\Phi$ as the concatenation of $\phi(s,a)$ over all $(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$ , and define the operator $P^{\pi}$ as

$$ \displaystyle(P^{\pi}f)(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sim P(s,a)\times\pi}f(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}). $$

We additionally define $\tilde{w}$ which satisfies the condition

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{w}= \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\left[\phi(s,a)\phi(s,a)^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1} \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\left[\phi(s,a)\left(r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sim P(s,a)\times\pi}\left[\phi(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})^{\top}\tilde{w}\right]\right)\right]\right), $$

and let $\tilde{Q}(s,a)=\phi(s,a)^{\top}\tilde{w}$ . It is straightforward to see that $\tilde{w}$ is the fixed point of the population (i.e., $n\to\infty$ ) projected least square update (19). Furthermore, note that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{w}= \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\left[\phi(s,a)\left(\phi(s,a)-\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sim P(s,a)\times\pi}\phi(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right)^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\left[\phi(s,a)r(s,a)\right]. $$

With this characterization, letting $\phi_{sup}:=\sup_{s,a}\|\phi(s,a)\|$ , we have $\|\tilde{w}\|=O\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}}\Upsilon_{2}^{-1}\right)$ . We define the operator $D_{\nu}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\|f\|_{\nu}^{2}=\langle f,D_{\nu}f\rangle, $$

and we omit the subscript when $\nu$ is the Lebesgue measure, and we also use $\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}$ and $\hat{P}^{\pi}$ to define the empirical counterpart of $\Pi_{\nu}$ and $P^{\pi}$ . With the update (19), we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Phi\hat{w}_{t+1}=\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}(r+\gamma\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi\hat{w}_{t}),\hskip 8.50012pt\Phi\tilde{w}=\Pi_{\nu}(r+\gamma P^{\pi}\Phi\tilde{w}), $$

which leads to

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(\tilde{w}-\hat{w}_{t+1})= \displaystyle(\Pi_{\nu}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu})r+\gamma(\Pi_{\nu}P^{\pi})\Phi(\tilde{w}-\hat{w}_{t}) \displaystyle+\gamma(\Pi_{\nu}P^{\pi}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi})\Phi\hat{w}_{t}. $$

With the triangle inequality, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Phi(\tilde{w}-\hat{w}_{t+1})\right\|_{\nu}\leqslant \displaystyle\gamma\left\|\Phi(\tilde{w}-\hat{w}_{t})\right\|_{\nu}+\left\|\left(\Pi_{\nu}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\right)r\right\|_{\nu} \displaystyle+\gamma\left\|\left(\Pi_{\nu}P^{\pi}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi\hat{w}_{t}\right\|_{\nu}, $$

where we use the contractivity under $\|\cdot\|_{\nu}$ . Telescoping gives

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Phi(\tilde{w}-\hat{w}_{T})\right\|_{\nu}\leqslant \displaystyle\gamma^{T}\left\|\Phi(\tilde{w}-\hat{w}_{0})\right\|_{\nu}\!+\!\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\left\|\left(\Pi_{\nu}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\right)r\right\|_{\nu} \displaystyle+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\max_{t\in[T]}\left\|\left(\Pi_{\nu}P^{\pi}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi\hat{w}_{t}\right\|_{\nu}. $$

Note that $\|\phi(s,a)\|={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}O(\phi_{\sup})}$ , and $\|\tilde{w}\|=O({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}}\Upsilon_{2}^{-1})$ . We follow the proof of Theorem 5.1 from [41] to bound the second term and the third term. In particular, as the subsequent analysis makes clear, the third term dominates the second term, so we focus on bounding the third term. For notational simplicity, we denote $w:=\hat{w}_{t}$ in this section. Note that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\left(\Pi_{\nu}P^{\pi}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi w\right\|_{\nu}\!=\!\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\left(\Pi_{\nu}P^{\pi}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Pi_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}-\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi w\right\|+\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\left(\Pi_{\nu}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\right)\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\| $$

For the first term, as $\Pi_{\nu}$ can be written as $\Pi_{\nu}=\Phi\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\Phi D_{\nu}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Pi_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}-\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\right\|\left\|\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\right\|\left\|\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}-\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle= \displaystyle O\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}}\Upsilon_{1}^{-1}\left\|\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}-\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi\right\|\|w\|\right). $$

For the second term, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\left(\Pi_{\nu}-\hat{\Pi}_{\nu}\right)\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\left(\!\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\!\right)^{-1}\Phi D_{\nu}\!-\!\left(\Phi^{\top}\hat{D}_{\nu}\!\Phi\right)^{-1}\Phi\hat{D}_{\nu}\right)\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\!\right\| \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\Phi\left(D_{\nu}-\hat{D}_{\nu}\right)\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle+\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\left(\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}-\left(\Phi^{\top}\hat{D}_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\right)\Phi\hat{D}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\|. $$

For the former term, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\Phi\left(D_{\nu}-\hat{D}_{\nu}\right)\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\right\|\left\|\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\right\|\left\|\Phi(D_{\nu}-\hat{D}_{\nu})\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle= \displaystyle O\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}}\Upsilon_{1}^{-1}\left\|\Phi(D_{\nu}-\hat{D}_{\nu})\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi\right\|\|w\|\right). $$

For the latter term, note that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{\!\!-1}\!\!-\!\!\left(\!\Phi^{\top}\hat{D}_{\nu}\Phi\!\right)^{\!\!-\!1}\!\!=\!\!(\!\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\!)^{\!\!-\!1}\left(\!\Phi^{\top}\left(\!\hat{D}_{\nu}\!\!-\!\!D_{\nu}\!\right)\Phi\!\right)(\!\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\!)^{\!\!-\!1}. $$

Hence, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|D_{\nu}^{1/2}\Phi\left(\left(\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}-\left(\Phi^{\top}\hat{D}_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\right)\Phi\hat{D}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi w\right\| \displaystyle= \displaystyle O\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}^{3}}\Upsilon_{1}^{-1}\left\|\Phi^{\top}\left(\hat{D}_{\nu}-D_{\nu}\right)\Phi\right\|\left\|\left(\Phi^{\top}\hat{D}_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\right\|\|w\|\right) $$

Now we bound the remaining terms $\left\|\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}-\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi\right\|$ , $\left\|\Phi(D_{\nu}-\hat{D}_{\nu})\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi\right\|$ and $\left\|\Phi^{\top}\left(\hat{D}_{\nu}-D_{\nu}\right)\Phi\right\|$ with standard concentration inequalities. We start with $\left\|\Phi^{\top}\left(\hat{D}_{\nu}-D_{\nu}\right)\Phi\right\|$ . Using the matrix Azuma inequality[50],

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Phi^{\top}\left(\hat{D}_{\nu}-D_{\nu}\right)\Phi\right\|=\tilde{O}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}^{2}}n^{-1/2}\right). $$

Hence, for sufficient large $n$ , we have that $\left\|\left(\Phi^{\top}\hat{D}_{\nu}\Phi\right)^{-1}\right\|=O(\Upsilon_{1}^{-1})$ . Moreover, as $\hat{P}^{\pi}$ is a stochastic operator, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Phi(D_{\nu}-\hat{D}_{\nu})\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi\right\|=\tilde{O}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}}n^{-1/2}\right). $$

Now we turn to the term $\left\|\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}-\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi\right\|$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\!\Phi^{\top}D_{\nu}\left(P^{\pi}\!\!-\!\!\hat{P}^{\pi}\right)\Phi\!\right\|\!\leqslant\!\left\|\Phi(D_{\nu}\!-\!\hat{D}_{\nu})\hat{P}^{\pi}\Phi\right\|\!+\!\left\|\!\Phi\left(\hat{D}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}\!-\!D_{\nu}P^{\pi}\right)\Phi\!\right\|. $$

We already have the bound for the first term. For the second term, we still apply the matrix Azuma’s inequality and obtain

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Phi\left(\hat{D}_{\nu}\hat{P}^{\pi}-D_{\nu}P^{\pi}\right)\Phi\right\|=\tilde{O}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}^{2}}n^{-1/2}\right). $$

Thus for large enough $n$ , we have $\|w\|:=\|\hat{w}_{t}\|=\Theta(\|\tilde{w}\|)$ . Combining the previous results completes the proof. ∎

### VI-E Detailed Proof for Lemma 12

Note that $\|\phi(s,a)\|_{2}=O({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}})$ and $\|\tilde{w}\|_{2}=O({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}\Upsilon_{2}^{-1}})$ . By Remark 6.7 in [35], we know that $\log\pi(a|s)$ is smooth with the smoothness parameter $\beta=O({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}^{2}})$ . As a result,

$$ \displaystyle\log\frac{\pi_{k+1}(a|s)}{\pi_{k}(a|s)}\geqslant\eta\left(\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{k}(a|s)\right)^{\top}\hat{w}_{k,T}-\frac{\eta^{2}\beta}{2}\left\|\hat{w}_{k,T}\right\|_{2}^{2}. $$

With this inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}}}\left[\mathrm{KL}(\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)\|\pi_{k}(\cdot|s))-\mathrm{KL}(\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)\|\pi_{k+1}(\cdot|s))\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{k+1}(a|s)}{\pi_{k}(a|s)}\right] \displaystyle\geqslant \displaystyle\eta\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left(\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{k}(a|s)\right)^{\top}\hat{w}_{k,T}\right]-\frac{\eta^{2}\beta}{2}\left\|\hat{w}_{k,T}\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\eta\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[A^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\right]-\frac{\eta^{2}\beta}{2}\left\|\hat{w}_{k,T}\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle+\eta\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left(\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{k}(a|s)\right)^{\top}\hat{w}_{k,T}-A^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1-\gamma)\eta\left(V^{\tilde{\pi}}-V^{\pi_{k}}\right)-\frac{\eta^{2}\beta}{2}\left\|\hat{w}_{k,T}\right\|_{2}^{2}-\eta\mathrm{err}_{k}, $$

where in the last step we use the performance difference lemma (Lemma 3.2 in [35]). Telescoping over $k$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\left\{V^{\tilde{\pi}}-V^{\pi_{k}}\right\}\leqslant \displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}}}\left[\mathrm{KL}(\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)\|\pi_{0}(\cdot|s)))\right]}{1-\gamma} \displaystyle+\frac{\eta^{2}\beta}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\left\|\hat{w}_{k,T}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathrm{err}_{k}. $$

Note that $\mathrm{KL}(\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)\|\pi_{0}(\cdot|s))\leqslant\log|\mathcal{A}|$ and $\left\|\hat{w}_{k,T}\right\|=O\left(\|\tilde{w}\|\right)=O({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\phi_{\sup}}\Upsilon_{2}^{-1})$ , we finish the proof. ∎

### VI-F Detailed Proof for Theorem 2

With Lemma 12 and our choice of $\eta$ , we only need to bound the term $\mathrm{err}_{k}$ . We observe that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{err}_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[A^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{w}_{k,T}}^{\top}\left(\phi(s,a)-\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k}(s)}\left[\phi(s,a^{\prime})\right]\right)\right] $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[A^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{w}_{k,T}}^{\top}\left(\phi(s,a)-\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{k}(s)}\left[\phi(s,a^{\prime})\right]\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[Q^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{Q}_{T}}^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\right] \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot|s)}\left[Q^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{Q}_{T}}^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\right] \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left(Q^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{Q}_{T}}^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\right)^{2}\right]} \displaystyle+\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\tilde{\pi}},a\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot|s)}\left[\left(Q^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{Q}_{T}}^{\pi_{k}}(s,a)\right)^{2}\right]}. $$

Plugging in $\pi^{*}$ as $\tilde{\pi}$ , combining the results in the previous subsection, we have concluded the proof. ∎

### VI-G Bounding the norms of $\psi_{rf}(s,a)$ and $\psi_{nys}(s,a)$

We have the following lemma which bounds the norm of $\|\psi_{rf}(s,a)\|$ and $\|\psi_{nys}(s,a)\|$ .

#### Lemma 16.

The random features and Nystrom features constructed in Algorithm 2 satisfy the bounds

$$ \displaystyle\ \left\lVert\psi_{rf}(s,a)\right\rVert\leqslant\sqrt{m}\tilde{g}_{\alpha} \displaystyle\ \|\psi_{nys}(s,a)\|\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{n_{nys}\tilde{g}_{\alpha}^{2}}{\lambda_{m}}} $$

respectively, where $\lambda_{m}$ denotes the $m$ -th largest eigenvalue of $K^{(n_{nys})}$ .

#### Proof.

Recall that

$$ \displaystyle\ \psi_{rf}(s,a):=\{\frac{g_{\alpha}(f(s,a))}{\alpha^{d}}\cos(\omega_{i}^{\top}f(s,a)+b_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m} \displaystyle\ \psi_{nys}(s,a):=\{\frac{g_{\alpha}(f(s,a))}{\alpha^{d}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{nys}}U_{\ell,i}k_{\alpha}\left(x_{\ell},\frac{f(s,a)}{1-\alpha^{2}}\right)\}_{i=1}^{m}, $$

where we recall that $U\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{nys}\times n_{nys}}$ is the $U$ that appears in the eigendecomposition of the empirical Nystrom Gram matrix $K^{(nys)}=U\Lambda U^{T}$ .

For random features, it is not hard to see that $\left\lVert\psi_{rf}(s,a)\right\rVert=O(\sqrt{m}\tilde{g}_{\alpha})$ , since each random feature takes the form of a randomly shifted cosine $\frac{g_{\alpha}(f(s,a))}{\alpha^{d}}$ , which in our paper is upper bounded by the expression $\tilde{g}_{\alpha}$ .

For notational convenience, we denote

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{K}_{\alpha}:=\begin{bmatrix}k_{\alpha}(x_{1},f(s,a))\\
\dots\\
k_{\alpha}(x_{n_{nys}},f(s,a))\end{bmatrix}. $$

Then, for Nystrom features, we note that since $0\leqslant k_{\alpha}(\cdot,\cdot)\leqslant 1$ and $U$ is an orthonormal matrix, we see that

$$ \displaystyle\ \|\psi_{nys}(s,a)\|^{2} \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \tilde{g}_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\tilde{K}_{\alpha}^{\top}U_{:,:m}\Lambda_{m}^{-1}U_{:,:m}^{\top}\tilde{K}_{\alpha}\right) \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ \tilde{g}_{\alpha}^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\lambda_{m}}\left(\tilde{K}_{\alpha}^{\top}U_{:,:m}U_{:,:m}^{\top}\tilde{K}_{\alpha}\right) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{(a)}}}{{\mathstrut{\leqslant}}} \displaystyle\ \frac{1}{\lambda_{m}}\tilde{g}_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\left\|\tilde{K}_{\alpha}\right\|^{2}\right) \displaystyle\leqslant \displaystyle\ n_{nys}\frac{1}{\lambda_{m}}\tilde{g}_{\alpha}^{2} $$

where we note that $U_{:,:m}$ denotes the first $m$ columns of $U$ , $\Lambda_{m}$ denoted the top $m$ by $m$ block of $\Lambda$ ,and we used independence of the columns of $U$ to derive (VI-G). Thus, for Nystrom features, we have the bound $\|\psi_{nys}(s,a)\|\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{n_{nys}\tilde{g}_{\alpha}^{2}}{\lambda_{m}}}$ . ∎

### VI-H Proofs of Lemmas 7, 8,9

#### Lemma 17 (Restatement of Lemma 7).

The random features $\psi_{rf}(s,a)$ are linearly independent almost surely, i.e. the probability of randomly drawing $\{\omega_{i},b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}\sim N(0,\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}I_{d})\times U([0,2\pi])$ is 0.

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, we consider the case that $\alpha=0$ , such that the random features take the form $\psi_{rf}(s,a)=\{\cos(\omega_{i}^{\top}f(s,a)+b_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}$ , where $\omega_{i}\sim N(0,\sigma^{-2}I_{d})$ and $b_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,2\pi])$ , i.e. the random features are randomly shifted cosines; we note that the general case when $\alpha>0$ can be easily reduced to this case since the factor $g_{\alpha}(f(s,a))/\alpha^{d}$ shared by all the features is strictly positive. Suppose the random features are not linearly independent over the space $f(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})$ . Then there exist scalars $\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}$ , not all of which are 0, such that

$$ S(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}^{\top}x+b_{i})=0,\quad\forall x\in f(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}). $$

Pick some $x^{0}$ in the interior of $f(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})$ , and denote $y_{i}:=\cos(\omega_{i}^{\top}x^{0}+b_{i})$ ; the fact that $x^{0}$ lies in the interior of $f(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})$ means that all derivatives of $S(x)$ vanish at $x=x^{0}$ . Now, for any natural number $n\leqslant m-1$ , differentiate $S(x)$ with respect to the first coordinate $x_{1}$ at the point $x^{0}$ , giving us

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}(\omega_{i})_{1}^{2n}y_{i}=0. $$

This then yields the following relation

$$ \displaystyle Va=0,\ \mbox{ where }\!V\!:=\!\begin{pmatrix}1&\dots&1\\
(\omega_{1})_{1}^{2}&\dots&(\omega_{m})_{1}^{2}\\
\vdots&\dots&\vdots\\
\left((\omega_{1})_{1}^{2}\right)^{m-1}&\dots&\left((\omega_{m})_{1}^{2}\right)^{m-1}\end{pmatrix},\ a:=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}\\
\vdots\\
a_{m}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $V\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ is a Vandermonde matrix, its determinant is non-zero so long as the $(\omega_{i})_{1}$ ’s are all distinct, which happens with probability 1 if the $\omega_{i}$ ’s are drawn iid from a Gaussian distribution. This implies then that the scalars $\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}$ must all be 0, which is a contradiction. Thus, the random features must be linearly independent over the space $f(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})$ . ∎

#### Lemma 18 (Restatement of Lemma 8).

Consider any feature dimension $0<m\leqslant n_{Nys}$ . Suppose the Nystrom Gram matrix $K^{(n_{Nys})}$ has rank at least $m$ . Then, the Nystrom features $\psi_{nys}(s,a)$ are linearly independent.

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, for simplicity we consider the case when $\alpha=0$ , in which case the Nystrom features are constructed as follows. First, let $m$ denote the feature dimension, and let $n_{nys}\geqslant m$ denote the number of random samples $\left\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n_{nys}}\right\}$ drawn from $\mathcal{S}$ following the distribution $\mu_{Nys}$ . Recall that the ( $n_{nys}$ by $n_{nys}$ ) Gram matrix $K$ is constructed as follows: $K_{i,j}=k(x_{i},x_{j}):=\exp\left(-\frac{-\|x_{i},x_{j}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right).$ Compute the eigendecomposition $KU=\Lambda U$ , where $UU^{\top}=U^{\top}U=I$ , and $\Lambda$ denoting a diagonal matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}\geqslant\dots\geqslant\lambda_{n_{nys}}\geqslant 0$ . Suppose that $m$ -th largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{m}>0$ . Then, for any $(s,a)$ pair,the $m$ Nystrom feature functions are given as

$$ (\psi_{nys})_{i}(s,a):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{nys}}U_{\ell,i}k(x_{\ell},f(s,a)),\quad\quad i\in[m]. $$

Note that by construction, the $m$ eigenvectors $U_{:,\ell}$ are linearly independent (so long as $\lambda_{m}>0)$ . Suppose that the $m$ Nystrom feature functions are not linearly independent. That implies then that there exists $m$ scalars $\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}\subset\mathbb{R}$ (at least some of which are nonzero) such that for any $(s,a)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}(\psi_{nys})_{i}(s,a)=0 \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{nys}}U_{\ell,i}k(x_{\ell},f(s,a))\right)=0 \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle\ \sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{nys}}k(x_{\ell},f(s,a))\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{nys}}U_{\ell,i}\right)\right)=0. $$

Note that since $k(\cdot,\cdot)>0$ , the above derivation implies that we must have for every $\ell\in[n_{nys}]$ :

$$ \displaystyle\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_{nys}}U_{\ell,i}\right)=0\implies\ U_{:,:m}\Lambda_{m}^{-1/2}a=0, $$

where $U_{:,:m}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{nys}\times m}$ denotes the first $m$ columns of $U$ , $\Lambda_{m}$ denotes the top $m$ by $m$ block of $\Lambda$ , and $a:=\mathrm{vec}(a_{1},\dots,a_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . Since the columns in $U$ are linearly independent by design, and $\Lambda_{m}\succ 0$ (by our assumption that $\lambda_{m}>0$ ), it follows that the vector $a\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ has to be 0, which contradicts the assumption that the $m$ Nystrom features are linearly dependent. Thus, whenever $\lambda_{m}>0$ , it follows that the Nystrom features are linearly independent.

∎

#### Lemma 19 (Restatement of Lemma 9).

Suppose the features $\phi(s,a)$ are linearly independent over the interior of the set $\mathrm{supp}(\nu^{\pi})$ for any policy $\pi$ . Then, for all but finitely many $0\leqslant\lambda<1$ , Assumption 3 holds.

#### Proof.

Fix a policy $\pi$ . Suppose the matrix $\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}\big[\psi(s,a)\psi(s,a)^{\top}\big]$ (which is positive-semidefinite) is not positive definite. Then, there exists some $0\neq v\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that

$$ v^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}\big[\psi(s,a)\psi(s,a)^{\top}\big]v=0. $$

This implies $v^{\top}\psi(s,a)=0$ for any $(s,a)\in\mathrm{int}(\mathrm{supp}(\nu^{\pi}))$ . However, by linear independence of the features $\{\psi_{i}(s,a)\}_{i=1}^{m}$ over $\mathrm{int}(\mathrm{supp}(\nu^{\pi}))$ , it follows that $v$ must be 0. This is a contradiction, and so the matrix $\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}\big[\psi(s,a)\psi(s,a)^{\top}\big]$ must be positive definite. Next, we show

$$ \sigma_{\min}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}\big[\psi(s,a)\big(\psi(s,a)-\gamma\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}[\psi(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})]\big)^{\top}\big]\right)>0 $$

for all but finitely many $0\leqslant\lambda<1$ . Denote the matrix $M(\lambda):=\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}\big[\psi(s,a)\big(\psi(s,a)-\gamma\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}[\psi(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})]\big)^{\top}\big]$ . Observe that the determinant of $M(\lambda)$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ with degree at most $m$ . Since $M(0)\neq 0$ (as we just showed that the matrix $\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{\pi}}\big[\psi(s,a)\psi(s,a)^{\top}\big]$ is positive definite), it follows that $\det(M(\lambda))$ is not the zero polynomial. Thus, it has at most $m$ roots, which shows that for all but finitely many $\lambda$ , $M(\lambda)$ must be invertible, i.e. its smallest singular value is bounded away from 0. ∎
